final_answer: The 2008 financial crisis was triggered by a series of interconnected issues. Subprime mortgage lending, which targeted borrowers with poor credit, expanded rapidly due to lax lending standards and rising housing prices. These mortgages were bundled into mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and collateralized debt obligations (CDOs), which were sold to investors. Rating agencies gave these complex financial products high credit ratings, masking their risk. As housing prices peaked and then collapsed, borrowers defaulted on loans, causing MBS and CDOs to lose value. Banks and financial institutions holding these assets faced massive losses, leading to liquidity crises. The collapse of Lehman Brothers in September 2008 marked a turning point, eroding confidence and freezing credit markets. Governments intervened with bailouts and stimulus to stabilize the system, but the crisis resulted in widespread bank failures, a global recession, and lasting economic repercussions.
